source_text: Quid igitur mihi responderis prudens et sollicitus auditor expendat. De parvulis certe agimus, quibus nulla propriae mentis adest voluntas, de quibus quaeritur per quid sint sub diabolo, quos Deus fecit, cum nihil mali ipsos egisse consentias. Tu eos concionatus es, ad ius daemonis propter peccatum, non propter naturam pertinere. Ad hoc insurrexit nostra responsio: Sed ut non potest esse sine sexibus fetus, ita nec sine voluntate delictum. Ad quod tu retulisti: Ita vero, ita est; id est, non potest esse sine voluntate delictum. Verum qui hoc confirmaveras, qua impudentia subdidisti: Sed per unum hominem peccatum intravit in mundum, per unius illius voluntatem?
pass_a_gloss: What therefore you have replied to me let a prudent and anxious hearer weigh. We treat certainly of little ones, for whom no will of their own mind is present, about whom it is asked through what they are under the devil, whom God made, when you consent that they themselves have done nothing of evil. You harangued that they belong to the demon's right on account of sin, not on account of nature. To this our reply rose: But as there cannot be offspring without sexes, so neither offense without will. To which you reported: So indeed, so it is; that is, there cannot be offense without will. But you who had confirmed this, by what shamelessness did you subjoin: But through one man sin entered into the world, through that one's will?

lemmas.lexica: LS voluntas=will, wish; Blaise moral will
LS peccatum=fault, error; Blaise Christian sin
LS/Blaise natura=created constitution, not 'original sin' itself
LS parvulus; Blaise infants as Julian's test case
LS malum; Blaise malum naturale vs malum voluntatis

pass_b_english: Let the thoughtful and attentive hearer weigh what you answered me. We are certainly discussing infants, who possess no will of their own minds. The question is through what they are under the devil, when God made them and you agree that they themselves have done nothing evil. You proclaimed that they belong to the demon’s jurisdiction because of sin, not because of nature. My reply rose against this: “But just as offspring cannot exist without the sexes, so an offense cannot exist without will.” (Romans 5:12) You answered, “Indeed, that is so”—that is, an offense cannot exist without will. But after confirming this, with what shamelessness did you add, “Yet through one man sin entered the world, through that one man’s will” (compare Romans 5:12)?

choices.why: Julian's definition of sin is an act of will. Keep 'will' rather than later 'free will' system language unless liberum arbitrium is present.
Julian's charge against Augustine: treating evil as a nature rather than as will.
Julian's forensic/moral fault tied to will, not a substance in nature.

anf_compare.notes: Victorian English of some of Julian survives inside NPNF Augustine (chiefly On Marriage and Concupiscence and related anti-Pelagian books). NPNF was not copied. Pass A is a literal gloss of Augustinus.it Latin of Julian's words only; Augustine's replies in the same locus are excluded.

bible_refs.note: From Pass B Scripture tagging; wording follows Julian's Latin, not a modern Bible.

speaker: Julian of Eclanum (words preserved in Augustine, Opus imperfectum contra Iulianum); Augustine's reply at this locus is excluded.
